data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Writers almost never say things the plain way. "I was nervous" is true, but "my stomach was a washing machine on spin cycle" is *felt*. Today you learn the tools — then use them.

1. Read **The Sideways Sentence** and watch for the five tools in action.
2. Learn the terms in the **Glossary**, then win the **Crossword**.
3. Keep the **Say It Sideways** chart nearby — it holds all five tools with an example each.
4. Sort the examples in **Name That Tool** — some are trickier than they look.
5. Take the quiz — it asks you to explain MEANING, not just name types.
6. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your own. This is the real work.
7. Read the FAQ if you are wondering where the weird idioms come from.
8. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Five Tools** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
9. Finish with **Design Challenge: Rewrite the Flat Announcement** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

Challenge: your last frame asks for an original metaphor about school. Make it one nobody has written before. ✍️🎭

history.title: The Sideways Sentence
history.data:
## The Sideways Sentence

The first day of school, Marisol's stomach was a washing machine on spin cycle.

That sentence is a lie. Her stomach was not actually an appliance. And yet you understood it instantly — probably better than if I had written "Marisol felt nervous." That is the strange power of **figurative language**: saying something untrue on purpose to deliver a truth faster.

Writers have five favorite tools.

A **simile** compares two unlike things using *like* or *as*. "The hallway was as loud as a stadium." You know the hallway is not a stadium, but now you can hear it.

A **metaphor** does the same comparison without the warning label — it just says one thing *is* another. "The hallway was a stadium." Stronger, because it does not apologize.

**Personification** hands human abilities to things that do not have them. "The old locker groaned when she opened it." Lockers cannot groan. But you heard that sound, did you not?

**Hyperbole** (say it: hy-PER-buh-lee) is exaggeration so extreme nobody could mistake it for fact. "I have told you a million times." The point is not the number. The point is the frustration.

An **idiom** is a phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from the words themselves. "Marisol decided to bite the bullet and raise her hand." No bullets. No biting. Every language has hundreds of these, and they are the hardest part of learning a new one — because you cannot reason your way to them, you simply have to learn them.

Here is what all five share: they ask the reader to do a little work. Your brain has to leap from *washing machine* to *nervous*, and that leap is what makes the sentence stick. Plain writing hands you the meaning. Figurative writing makes you catch it — and you remember what you catch.

So when you write, try saying it sideways once in a while. Not on every line, or your reader gets exhausted. But when a feeling really matters, do not tell them she was nervous. Show them the washing machine.

data.def: A comparison of two unlike things using the word like or as.
A comparison that says one thing IS another, with no like or as.
Giving human qualities or actions to something that is not human.
Exaggeration so extreme that nobody would take it literally.
A common phrase whose meaning cannot be figured out from the individual words.
Meaning exactly what the words say, with no comparison or exaggeration.
Meaning something different from the exact words, usually through comparison.
Language that creates a picture or a feeling in the reader's mind.
To show how two things are alike.
Something that stands for a bigger idea, like a dove standing for peace.

data.title: Remember the Five Tools
data.instructions: Each card locks in a tool from The Sideways Sentence. Study the example aid, make it yours, and explain how it leads back to what the tool does.
data.sourceExcerpt: A simile compares two unlike things using like or as. A metaphor does the same comparison without the warning label. An idiom is a phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from the words themselves.

cards.target: The five tools: simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, idiom
essentialFacts: Simile compares with like or as.
Metaphor says one thing is another.
Personification gives human actions to non-human things.
Hyperbole exaggerates so far nobody believes it.
Idiom is a phrase whose meaning you cannot build from its words.
cards.aiExample: S-M-P-H-I: Some Metaphors Paint Huge Images. Simile, Metaphor, Personification, Hyperbole, Idiom.
cards.mapping: Five words, five tools, and the sentence is itself figurative (metaphors do not literally paint), which is a small reminder of what the tools do.
scaffoldSteps: Write the five tools and circle S, M, P, H, I.
Build a sentence; bonus if it uses one of the tools.
Attach one example from the reading to each letter.
coachPrompts: Which letter is the tool you have to memorize rather than reason out, and does your sentence hint at that?
cards.reasoningPrompt: Explain how each word points to a tool and what it does.

hookFact.text: Figurative language says something untrue on purpose to deliver a truth faster.

cards.target: Simile versus metaphor: the warning label
essentialFacts: A simile compares two unlike things using like or as: 'as loud as a stadium.'
A metaphor makes the same comparison without like or as: 'the hallway was a stadium.'
A metaphor is stronger because it does not apologize.
cards.aiExample: SIMILE has an L in it, LIKE the L in LIKE. METAPHOR has no L: no like, no as, it just IS.
cards.mapping: The letter L is the hook: the tool with the L uses the word with the L. If the sentence has no like or as, it is the tool without the L.
cards.scaffoldStarter: Simile has ____, like the word ____. Metaphor has ____, so it just ____.
scaffoldSteps: Find the letter or sound that links simile to like or as.
Say what a metaphor does instead.
Rewrite one simile from the reading as a metaphor.
coachPrompts: Using your hook, which of the two is 'time is a thief'?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own letter or sound hook.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your hook show the only difference between the two tools?

hookFact.text: 'The hallway was a stadium.' Stronger, because it does not apologize.

cards.target: Idioms cannot be reasoned out; they must be learned
essentialFacts: An idiom's meaning cannot be worked out from the words themselves.
'Bite the bullet' has no bullets and no biting.
Idioms are the hardest part of learning a new language because you simply have to learn them.
Other languages have different idioms for the same idea.
cards.aiExample: An idiom is a locked box with a family combination. You cannot pick the lock by staring at the words; someone hands you the code, and after that you open it instantly.
cards.mapping: The box is the phrase, the code is the learned meaning, and the fact that staring does not help maps to the reading's point that you cannot reason your way to an idiom.
cards.scaffoldStarter: An idiom is like a ____ with a ____. You cannot ____ by looking; someone has to ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick something you can only use once someone tells you how (a password, a secret handshake).
Map the phrase and the meaning onto it.
Test it with 'raining cats and dogs.'
coachPrompts: Using your analogy, why are idioms so hard for someone learning English?
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your analogy separate idioms from the other four tools?

history.title: Meaning, Not Just Names

questions.question: "The old house wheezed every time the wind blew." Which tool is this, and why?
options: Simile — it compares the house to a person using like
Hyperbole — it exaggerates how windy it was
Idiom — wheezing house is a common saying
Personification — a house cannot wheeze, but people can
questions.correctAnswer: Personification — a house cannot wheeze, but people can

questions.question: What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor?
options: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor states the comparison directly
A simile is about people; a metaphor is about objects
A simile is true; a metaphor is false
A metaphor is longer than a simile
questions.correctAnswer: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor states the comparison directly

questions.question: "My little sister is a tornado in the morning." What does this actually tell you about her?
options: She is dangerous and should be avoided
She is loud, fast, and leaves a mess behind her
She is interested in weather
She spins in circles when she wakes up
questions.correctAnswer: She is loud, fast, and leaves a mess behind her

questions.question: Why are idioms especially hard for someone learning a new language?
options: They use bigger vocabulary words than other sentences
They are always spoken very quickly
Their meaning cannot be worked out from the words themselves
They only appear in old books
questions.correctAnswer: Their meaning cannot be worked out from the words themselves

questions.question: Which sentence is LITERAL (not figurative)?
options: The temperature dropped to 41 degrees last night
The night wrapped the town in a cold blanket
It was freezing enough to turn me into a popsicle
The cold bit at my fingers
questions.correctAnswer: The temperature dropped to 41 degrees last night

questions.question: Rewrite this plain sentence twice — once with a simile and once with a metaphor: "The cafeteria was noisy."
questions.expectedAnswer: Simile: The cafeteria was as noisy as a stadium during a goal (uses like or as). Metaphor: The cafeteria was a stadium at kickoff (states it directly). Both compare the noise to something louder without using the word noisy.

questions.question: The reading says figurative language 'asks the reader to do a little work.' Explain what that means and why it helps a reader remember.
questions.expectedAnswer: The reader has to figure out the connection themselves — for example, leaping from washing machine to nervous. Because your brain does that work instead of just receiving the meaning, the image sticks in memory.

reflections.text: What is a phrase your family says that would sound strange to someone outside your family? What does it really mean?
Describe your mood this morning using a metaphor — no explaining allowed, just the image.

history.meta: 5 MCQ + 2 short answer • meaning over labeling

items.text: When I am nervous, my ____ feels like ____.
My favorite place is ____ — it IS ____. (metaphor, no like or as)

history.title: Where Do Weird Sayings Come From?

data.question: Why do we say 'it's raining cats and dogs'? 🐱🐶
data.answer: Nobody knows for sure, which is honest and a little unsatisfying. The best guesses involve heavy storms washing debris (and unlucky animals) through old city streets. Historians disagree, so treat any confident answer with suspicion.

data.question: Is 'break a leg' really about wishing someone luck?
data.answer: Yes — theater people thought saying 'good luck' was unlucky, so they said the opposite. Many idioms come from superstitions like this.

data.question: Can a metaphor be wrong? 🤨
data.answer: It can be *bad* — confusing, or comparing things with nothing in common. 'My homework is a refrigerator' does not click, because we cannot find the connection. Good metaphors share something real.

data.question: Do other languages have the same idioms?
data.answer: Almost never the same ones! Spanish speakers might say it is raining jugs; German speakers, that it is raining young dogs. Same idea, completely different picture.

data.question: Is hyperbole the same as lying?
data.answer: No, because nobody is meant to believe it. If you say a backpack weighs a thousand pounds, no one goes looking for a scale. A lie is meant to be believed; hyperbole is meant to be felt.

data.question: Why do teachers want us to use this stuff so much?
data.answer: Because it is evidence you understand something well enough to compare it to something else. Anyone can define nervous. Only someone who has *felt* it invents the washing machine.

history.title: Design Challenge: Rewrite the Flat Announcement
history.meta: 5th Grade • Design brief • make a dull school notice felt, not just read

data.title: Rewrite the Flat Announcement
data.instructions: Take a real, dull school announcement and redesign it so readers feel it, using at least three of the five tools on purpose. Then test it on real readers and revise the line that did not land.
data.fitReason: The reading's last paragraph tells writers when to say it sideways and when not to. A redesign of a real notice makes students choose tools for effect and notice when a tool exhausts the reader.

brief.context: The morning announcements are read aloud and nobody listens. The office has offered to read one student-written version of a real notice: the book fair, a recycling drive, a spirit day, or a reminder to return library books.
brief.audience: The whole school, listening over the speaker, and the office staff who will read it
brief.drivingQuestion: How can we rewrite one flat announcement so listeners feel it and remember it, using figurative language that lands, without exhausting them?
brief.seedDirection: Find the feeling first. What should a listener feel about the book fair? Then choose the tool that delivers that feeling fastest.
lockedLessonFacts: A simile compares two unlike things using like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.
Personification gives human actions to non-human things; hyperbole exaggerates so far nobody believes it; an idiom's meaning cannot be built from its words.
Figurative language asks the reader to do a little work, and that leap is what makes the sentence stick.
Plain writing hands you the meaning; figurative writing makes you catch it.
Not every line should be figurative, or the reader gets exhausted.
openQuestions: What is the one feeling this announcement should create?
Which tools work when heard aloud versus read on a page?
How many figurative lines can a 30-second announcement hold before it gets tiring?
Will everyone in the school understand the idiom we chose?
stakeholders: Younger students who may not know an idiom
The teacher or club whose event it is
criteria: Uses at least three different tools, each labeled in the design notes
Keeps every fact from the original notice (date, place, what to do)
At least one line is deliberately plain, with a note explaining why
Tested on at least three listeners with one line revised afterward
constraints: Nothing that could confuse a listener about the date or place
No inside jokes only your class gets
Idioms must be ones younger students know, or explained by context
brief.deliverable: The original notice, your rewritten version with each tool labeled, a 30-second timing, and a short test report: what three listeners remembered and which line you changed because of them.

parallelExample.context: A library wanted more kids at its summer reading kickoff, and its flyer said 'Summer Reading Program begins June 15.'
parallelExample.move: A student rewrote the headline as 'The library is about to wake up' (personification), kept the date and time exactly, and left the instructions plain so nobody missed how to sign up. Sign-ups doubled, and the librarian kept the plain instructions on purpose.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows the balance the reading asks for: one strong sideways line to make people feel it, and plain lines where the facts have to land.

supports.frameStarter: The original says ____. We want listeners to feel ____. So we wrote '____' (tool: ____), and we kept '____' plain because ____.
frameChoices: Open with a metaphor that names the feeling
Personify the event or the place
Use one hyperbole for humor, then get plain for the facts
Close with a simile listeners can picture
coachPrompts: Read it aloud. Where did your listeners' faces change?
Which line is figurative just because you could make it figurative?
Did anyone miss the date? Then a tool got in the way.

data.coachHint: One or two sideways lines make people listen. Five make them stop. Keep the facts plain and let the feeling do the rest.
data.sourceExcerpt: Try saying it sideways once in a while. Not on every line, or your reader gets exhausted. But when a feeling really matters, do not tell them she was nervous. Show them the washing machine.
